3856.dq: El acento tónico permanece invariablemente en la raiz principal de la palabra. Cuando ésta está formada de varias raices, cada una de ellas lleva el acento tónico, de lo que resulta que una palabra tiene uno, dos y mas acentos.

3856.prule: The tonic accent stays invariably on the principal root of the word; a word built from several roots carries one tonic accent per root, so a word has one, two or more accents. Because the language is prefixing and the principal root is generally the last syllable of the word (p. 4), the accent of a single-root word normally falls on the final syllable (kètsuè 'perro', accent on the final e). Position is set by morpheme identity (root vs. prefix/particle), not by syllable count or weight.
3856.srule: No secondary stress described; additional accents only in multi-root words: a word formed from several roots carries the tonic accent on each root, 'de lo que resulta que una palabra tiene uno, dos y mas acentos' (tchintsi tiòhò 'enredar': tsi and hó; tchininkià nawi 'envenenar': kiá and wi), with no ranking among them. Single-root words have one accent (on the root).

tn.quote: La lengua de los Amuzgos, como el trike, el chocho y el mazateco tiene por peculiar distinción en su prosodia cierto acento en las sílabas, que constituyen las palabras que no es dable representar con signos gráficos porque pertenecen al canto del idioma y manera particular de hablar de esta nación. Sin embargo dicho acento es esencial en esta lengua porque por él se distinguen muchas palabras que se escriben de igual manera, para cuya distinción se requiere oirlas de viva voz. ... El acento tónico permanece invariablemente en la raiz principal de la palabra.
tn.translation: The language of the Amuzgos, like Trique, Chocho and Mazatec, has as a peculiar distinction in its prosody a certain accent on the syllables that make up the words, which cannot be represented with graphic signs because they belong to the song of the language and this nation's particular way of speaking. Nevertheless this accent is essential in this language, because by it many words that are written the same way are distinguished, and to tell them apart one must hear them spoken aloud. ... The tonic accent remains invariably on the principal root of the word.

The Iquito word prosodic system consists of clearly distinguishable stress and tone systems, in which stress and tone have distinct acoustic correlates. [p. 54]

3857.heavy: C(y)V: syllables (long vowel, with or without a palatal glide) are heavy; the language has no closed syllables, so vowel length is the only weight contrast.

3857.prule: Feet are bimoraic (moraic) trochees parsed exhaustively right-to-left over the prosodic word; a long-vowel syllable C(y)V: is heavy, is always stressed and forms its own foot; the head of the rightmost foot carries primary stress. So primary stress is penultimate when the last two syllables are light ((ˈa.ʃi), (ˌku.ma)(ˈki.ha)), final when the final syllable is heavy (nu(ˌta.ku)(ˈrɨɨ), (ˌii)(ˈpɨɨ)), and on a heavy penult before a light final, which forms a trimoraic (ˈHL) foot rather than a final degenerate foot ((ˈsaa.pi)). Degenerate (monomoraic) feet are never built at the right edge (*(ˌL)(ˈL), *(ˌH)(ˈL)). Stress is diagnosed by tapping tasks and by lengthening of the post-tonic consonant, not by pitch.
3857.srule: Secondary stress on the head of every non-final foot of the right-to-left moraic-trochee parse: alternating leftward from the primary over light syllables, and on every non-final heavy (CV:) syllable ((ˌkana)(ˌnahu)(ˈkura), (ˌmɨɨ.sɨ)(ˈyɨ.ka), (ˌii)(ˈpɨɨ)); a leftover initial light syllable is unstressed (nu(ˌtaki)(ˈnaka)) except when stressing it as a degenerate foot makes the word dipodic ((ˌka)(ˈha.ʃi), (ˌma)(ˈhuu), (ˌmɨ)(ˈtii.ha)).
3857.quote: For the most part, the Iquito stress system is relatively simple, consisting of right-to-left exhaustively parsed moraic trochees. The language generally does not permit degenerate feet. 3857.tone: Iquito also has a low-density privative H/ø tone system on the mora (§5, pp. 62-69), with lexical tonal minimal pairs. Every prosodic word must carry at least one H; when the rightmost colon has no lexical H, a metrical H is assigned to the primary-stressed syllable. tn.quote: Iquito exhibits a H/ø privative tone system in which the tone bearing unit is the mora. Moras are thus either specified as bearing a high tone, or are unspecified for tone. Most moras are in fact unspecified for tone ... All prosodic words in Iquito exhibit at least a single high tone, and if a given prosodic word lacks lexically specified high tones (a common occurrence), a high tone is assigned to the syllable bearing primary stress. In this way, the tonal system is partially dependent on the stress system of the language for meeting an obligatory tone requirement.

secx.sec_quote_tr: A suprasegmental property of the clause, which helps us determine the number or the limits of a clause in a context, is the accent. Each clause has one primary accent and one or more secondary accents. The primary accent almost always falls on the last word; above all when the clause stands at the end of a sentence with a mid or rising final cadence.

3867.dq: Phonological words contain syllables which are grouped together rhythmically and carry at least a third degree of stress. Phrase or clause stress may also occur on the same syllable obscurring the word stress.
3867.dloc: §2.1.6 'Level 6 - the phonological word', pp. 18-19; §2.2 Summary of Levels, p. 21.
3867.prule: Word stress on the first syllable of the (phonological) word: disyllables and trisyllables are stressed initially ('SS, 'SSS). Where a grammatical-word boundary falls after the first syllable of a two- or three-syllable phonological word, the stress sits on the second syllable, i.e. on the first syllable of the grammatical word (S'S, S'SS). Word stress is the third (lowest) degree in a clause > phrase > word stress hierarchy and may be obscured by phrase or clause stress.
3867.srule: Secondary stress on the third syllable of four-syllable words; longer words build a trochaic rhythm on the initial (primary) stress (Capell 1962, Jiwadja grammar section 1.7; occasional final stresses also noted, e.g. /ga'ralg/ 'his body'). 3868.prule: Primary stress falls on the final syllable of the word (= final syllable of the root; only proclitics exist), in words of every length ('sin importar la longitud'); fixed, predictable, quantity-insensitive, non-contrastive, demarcative; Spanish loans are re-stressed on the final syllable (bisiˈkleta -> bi2.si2.kle2.ˈta1). Stress and tone are independent: F0 is explicitly rejected as a stress correlate (p.231, 'se descarta que la tonía sea un correlato fonético importante para el acento'); stressed (final) tones are slightly lower by general declination; the patterns A.M, A.B, M.B are rare in the native lexicon (high tone attracted to the prominent final syllable, De Lacy 1999). The author codes stress as a separate, fixed, demarcative word-stress system, so the record is fixed and quantity-insensitive rather than tone or pitch accent.

3869.tone: Source calls yuhmu 'una lengua tonal' with three tones (H, L, LH) that distinguish words (Cuadro 61 minimal triplets) and proclitic particles (Rà 'el/la' vs Rá 'su', Cuadro 62). The only mention of accent in the whole 96-page text is p. 18 n. 2 ('solo se escribe el tono que recae en la sílaba acentuada'); the tone-bearing syllable is then located as the first/leftmost syllable of the word, with a prefixal ni- skipped. This is a tone description carrying an implicit accent statement (tone-bearing = accented = word/root-initial syllable), not a stress rule with correlates. The manual's own orthography writes tone on 'la primera sílaba de las palabras' (p. 57); the INALI hñähñu norm (2014) writes H with acute, L unmarked, LH with a double vowel.

3872.prule: Primary stress on the penultimate syllable of the word, quantity-insensitive, computed from syllable count only ('ya.ne, ya.'ne.mo, ko.ndo.wo.'te.to). Named exceptions: final-syllable stress on the last word of a phrase with interrogative intonation, and 'often' on the final syllable of a [+nasal] root (pa.'rá, pa.'rá.mi, pa.'rá.mi.mo).

3873.prule: Stress is non-contrastive and predictable from the phonetic tone sequence of a two-toneme (high/low) system: it falls on the first of a series of high tones, on the first part of a phonetic falling tone, on the first part of a phonetic rising tone (on the second part when the first vowel is high and the second non-high), and on the first syllable of a VV-shaped unit (the emphasizers). No positional, weight-based, lexical or morphological stress rule; stress is a correlate of tone.
3873.srule: Not mentioned in Williamson 1965 (sec. 1.6.3 Stress, p. 26, read in full; other stress mentions p. 29 question intonation and p. 109 English loans; in-book searches for 'secondary', 'unstressed', 'stresses', 'secondary stress' return nothing on secondary stress). The p. 26 'rhythm' sentence concerns timing (neither syllable-timed nor stress-timed; tone groups roughly isochronous), not secondary stresses.

Word-final long vowels never carry the accent (sáfarū, 'áni). Words with no such sequence take initial stress: KvKvK 'always' (no Ṣanʿāʾ-type final stress xuláb), KvKvKvK 'mostly' (kásilah, bágarah, gútilan).

3881.quote: [V&G 2013:101-102] Stress occurs once per word. Regular stress occurs on the second syllable of the word, as in /mi.ˈka.ra.waɁ/ ‘turkey’.
